title: For the travelers
hookLine: a delayed flight, a kid asleep across three chairs; Shantideva wishes every traveler a happy road and a safe return
tomorrow: how long would you promise to stay for someone?

lines: A WISH FOR EVERYONE AT THE GATE.
THE ROAD, THE GOAL, THE SHORE.
cards: Gate changed. Flight delayed, then delayed again. A kid asleep across three chairs.
Someone's charger stretched to the one outlet that works. A man at the desk, getting louder. Shantideva has a wish for every person at that gate.

May travelers find happiness on every road. May they reach what they set out for without a struggle. And for the ones at sea: may they come safely to the shore they hoped for, and be glad again with their families.

teach.b: Travel is an in-between. You're not where you were and not yet where you're going, and things you can't control decide your day. Buddhism has an old soft spot for the road.

teach.h: MAGGA: THE ROAD AND THE PATH.
teach.b: The suttas show the Buddha walking from town to town, teaching along the way, and in Pali the word for road, magga, is also the word for the path itself.
Shantideva's wish covers the whole trip: the road, the goal, and the coming home. And look who it's for. Not only the people you love.
Every traveler. The stranger with the crying baby. The driver who cut you off on the highway.
The man yelling at the gate desk, who might be about to miss a funeral or a birth, for all anyone knows. Here's what the tradition hands you for a travel day. Turn the waiting room around.
Instead of everyone being in your way, each one is someone with a road and a reason, and maybe a family waiting at the far end.

And when the one leaving is someone you love, the verse gives you something to do besides worry: wish them every road. Every road means the smooth ones and the detours, the long way and the wrong turn.

how: Buddhists may recite wishes for travelers before a journey or when a relative sets out; in Mahayana communities, Shantideva's dedication verses are read as wishes for everyone on the road.

o: a blessing for pilgrims visiting the Buddha's holy sites
a rule that monks must keep walking and never settle
wishing everyone on a journey a happy road and safe return

games.q: the traveler's wish — tap the pairs.
p: a safe shore, a glad homecoming

s: the traveler's wish is only for pilgrims on religious journeys
Shantideva wishes happiness to travelers on every road, wherever they're headed.
the wish covers the road, the goal and the safe return
the whole trip: happiness on the way, reaching the goal, coming home glad.
the wish is meant for the people you love, not strangers
it's for every traveler: the crying baby, the driver who cut you off, the man at the desk.

games.q: your flight is delayed four hours, and the man beside you is yelling at the gate agent. what does Shantideva's wish do here?
o: see him as a traveler too, with a road and a reason, and wish him well.
save the wish for people you know; strangers aren't your business.
move away; the verse is about journeys, not about rude people.
games.why: the wish is for every traveler. it doesn't excuse the yelling; it just stops the gate from being full of obstacles and fills it with people on roads.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly across the room and back, feeling each step land. With each step, bring to mind someone who is traveling, today or soon, a friend or a stranger, and wish them a good road.
If walking isn't possible, let your feet press the floor, one and then the other.

wordCard.voice: For the travelers: Shantideva's wish that everyone on the road finds happiness, reaches their goal and comes home safe.

orig.note: Pali: road, path. The same word names the Buddha's path itself.

carryVoice: Pocket this: every road, the detours too, for strangers as much as friends. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 10.20–10.22 (may travelers find happiness everywhere and accomplish their aims without effort; may those at sea reach the shore and rejoice with their relatives)
Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16 (the Buddha walking from village to village, teaching)
